summary: A white paper on engineering considerations for IPng relating to ATM services, submitted in response to RFC 1550. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A paper about making the new Internet design work well on fast ATM networks.

subtitle: Making a new Internet protocol work efficiently on fast ATM networks.

tldr.problem: Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) is an emerging high-speed link technology with sophisticated virtual circuit capabilities, but IPng needed to efficiently map application traffic flows to ATM virtual circuits for gigabit-per-second performance.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC identifies four types of ATM parameters that must be derivable from IPng packets: addressing (mapping to ATM addresses), quality-of-service parameters, connection management information, and a virtual circuit identifier that efficiently maps application flows to ATM circuits.
tldr.outcome: The analysis provided engineering guidance to ensure IPng proposals could support ATM's advanced features while maintaining compatibility with conventional network technologies.

facts.label: IP flow identification parameters
facts.value: 5 (src addr, dst addr, src port, dst port, protocol)

today: RFC 1680 is an informational document from 1994 reflecting the state of ATM technology and early IPng proposals. While IPv6 was eventually selected as IPng, the integration of IPv6 with ATM never achieved the sophisticated per-application virtual circuit mapping the RFC envisioned, as ATM did not achieve widespread adoption in enterprise networks.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
This white paper addresses engineering considerations for IPng support of ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) services. ATM is a sophisticated link-level technology providing virtual channel capabilities over a single physical wire or fiber, with customizable performance and quality of service characteristics for each channel.

Unlike conventional link technologies such as Ethernet that provide a single performance characteristic shared by all applications, ATM allows each virtual circuit to be customized for an application's specific network performance objectives. The future Internet is expected to be heterogeneous, with data passing through ATM networks alongside conventional technologies like Ethernet, FDDI, and HIPPI.

The RFC emphasizes that while initial IPng over ATM support may not facilitate a dedicated virtual circuit per application, the infrastructure must be designed to enable such mapping as ATM technology matures.
sections.plainLanguage: ATM is like a fancy highway where different cars can take custom-built lanes with different speed limits. IPng needs to tell ATM which lane an application should use and how fast each lane should go.

sections.title: ATM Characteristics and Services
sections.content:
ATM provides several differentiating characteristics. It allows many virtual channels over a single physical link, similar to X.25, but each channel can have customizable performance characteristics. ATM virtual circuits are established dynamically through a signaling protocol where a source initiates negotiation for connection establishment.

ATM signaling establishes "hard state" in network switching equipment, meaning the network maintains connection state and guarantees service. An ATM end system must actively manage connections by informing the network to establish, alter, or tear down connections.

Each ATM endpoint has a globally unique, hierarchical ATM address that supports dynamic connection establishment and eventual routing. The ATM UNI signaling protocol (ITU-TS Q.93B) allows specification of multiple service parameters including AAL information, network QOS objectives, connection traffic descriptors, and transit network selection.

Service classes defined by Q.93B include circuit emulation (Class A), variable bit rate audio and video (Class B), connection-oriented data (Class C), connectionless data (Class D), and best-effort service (Class X). Parameters can specify peak cell rate, sustainable cell rate, burst sizes, cell transfer delay, delay variation, and cell loss ratio.
sections.plainLanguage: ATM lets you create different virtual pipes, each with its own speed limit and reliability guarantees. Applications can ask for fast pipes for video or slow pipes for email, and ATM keeps track of what each pipe is doing.

sections.title: Parameters for Mapping IPng to ATM
sections.content:
Four types of ATM parameters must be derivable from IPng packets. Addressing parameters require mapping IPng addresses to ATM addresses and ATM routing information. This is similar to current IP over Ethernet address resolution and is addressed by protocols like "Classical IP over ATM."

Quality-of-Service parameters define an application's traffic characteristics and network performance objectives (delay, throughput requirements). These can only be specified by the application level, not the IPng level, since different applications have vastly different needs. A file transfer application requires high throughput and low error rates, while a time service could use best-effort delivery. Some QoS information might be derived from resource reservation protocols supporting integrated services.

Connection management information controls establishment and release of ATM connections. ATM signaling establishes hard state, making the ATM endpoint responsible for informing the network of state changes. IPng could support this through resource reservation protocols rather than directly in the IPng protocol.

A connection identifier must map IPng packets from an application to an ATM virtual circuit. Currently, IP uses five parameters to identify an application's traffic flow: source and destination IP addresses, source and destination TCP/UDP ports, and IP protocol identifier. This combination is complex and costly to implement at gigabit rates.

ATM provides 24 bits for virtual circuit identification (VPI and VCI), supporting 2^24 (approximately 16 million) connections. IPng's connection identifier should be large enough to map every application on an end system to a distinct ATM virtual circuit while remaining efficient to process at gigabit-per-second rates.
sections.plainLanguage: IPng packets need to carry four kinds of information: addresses for ATM to find the destination, speed and reliability requirements, instructions for setting up and tearing down connections, and a simple number that identifies which application owns each packet.

sections.title: Implementation and Heterogeneous Networks
sections.content:
An IPng candidate must demonstrate that mapping from an application's IPng packets to ATM virtual circuit(s) can be accomplished efficiently in a heterogeneous Internet architecture while supporting gigabit-per-second rates. The mapping mechanism must be simple and fast, not requiring complex computation on every packet.

The challenge is that applications traversing the Internet may pass through multiple network types. A data flow might originate on Ethernet, pass through an ATM network, traverse FDDI, pass through another ATM network, and arrive at a HIPPI destination. IPng must support ATM's advanced features while maintaining compatibility with these conventional subnetworks that offer only best-effort service.

The RFC emphasizes that careful consideration is needed for the complexity of the mapping algorithm given that IPng/ATM subnetworks will eventually operate at gigabit-per-second rates.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet traffic takes many different paths through different kinds of networks. IPng has to work with ATM's fancy per-application paths while still working on regular networks that treat all traffic the same way.
